questions.stem: Where should you download a web browser from to minimize the risk of a malicious version?
questions.explanation: Always download the browser directly from the developer's official website; malicious versions are often distributed on third-party sites.
questions.trap: Third-party aggregators and email links are exactly where trojaned installers spread.

questions.stem: To confirm a downloaded installer is authentic, the developer publishes a SHA-256 string. How do you verify the file?

choices.text: Check that the file name matches
Run the same hashing algorithm on your download and confirm the hashes match
Open the file in Notepad and read the header

questions.explanation: Hash verification: run the same algorithm (e.g. SHA-256) on your downloaded file; if the resulting hash matches the developer's published hash, the file is authentic and unmodified.
questions.trap: Matching file size or name proves nothing; an attacker can match both while altering content. The hash is what verifies integrity.

questions.stem: Why are browser extensions a major attack vector?

choices.text: They run in a fully isolated sandbox with no access to your data
They can only change the browser's theme
They are unable to read web pages
They have the same level of access to your system as the browser itself

questions.explanation: Extensions have the same level of access as the browser itself, so a malicious one can log keystrokes, steal passwords, and screenshot your data. Only install from trusted sources.
questions.trap: Extensions are not fully sandboxed away from your data - that's exactly why a bad one is so dangerous.

questions.stem: A browser shows 'Your connection is not private.' Besides an expired or mismatched certificate, what simple LOCAL cause should you check first?

choices.text: The computer's clock is set to the wrong date and time
The monitor brightness is too low

questions.explanation: A wrong system date/time is a common, simple cause of certificate warnings - the browser thinks the certificate is expired or not yet valid.
questions.trap: Brightness, keyboard layout, and zoom have nothing to do with certificate validation.

questions.stem: On a shared/public computer, which browser mode ensures no history, cookies, or cache are saved locally after the window closes?
questions.explanation: Private browsing mode ensures no history, cookies, or cache are saved to the local machine once you close the window - ideal for public/shared computers.
questions.trap: Full-screen and reader modes change display, not what is stored locally.

questions.stem: A website is rendering oddly and behaving inconsistently. Which routine browser-maintenance step is recommended because this stored data can become corrupted or outdated?

choices.text: Clear the browsing data, especially the cache

questions.explanation: The cache stores site data locally to speed things up, but it can become corrupted or outdated and cause issues, so periodically clear the browsing data/cache.
questions.trap: Disabling the pop-up blocker or adding extensions increases risk and doesn't fix corrupted cached data.

questions.stem: What is the recommended setting for a browser's pop-up blocker?

choices.text: Only block pop-ups on the home page
Keep it enabled and grant exceptions only to specific trusted sites

questions.explanation: Keep the pop-up blocker enabled and only grant exceptions to specific trusted sites that need them.
questions.trap: Allowing pop-ups everywhere reopens a common malware and scam vector.

questions.stem: In a corporate environment, which tool acts as a middleman that filters web traffic, can block malicious sites and scan for malware, and may require configuring an address and port in the browser?
questions.explanation: A proxy server is the middleman that filters all web traffic, can block malicious sites, scan for malware, and enforce access control; you may need to set its address and port in the browser.
questions.trap: A certificate authority issues/validates certificates; it does not proxy and filter your browsing traffic.

questions.stem: Which browser privacy feature encrypts DNS queries so others on the network cannot snoop on which sites you visit?
questions.explanation: Secure DNS, also known as DNS over HTTPS, encrypts your DNS queries so no one on the network can snoop on the sites you are visiting.
questions.trap: Private browsing only prevents LOCAL storage of history; it does not encrypt DNS queries on the network.

questions.stem: Why does the review recommend using a dedicated password manager alongside the browser?

choices.text: It replaces the need for HTTPS
It stores a unique complex password per site, neutralizing the risk of password reuse

questions.explanation: A password manager is an encrypted vault that stores a unique complex password for every site, so a breach of one site can't be reused against the others.
questions.trap: A password manager doesn't replace HTTPS; encryption in transit and credential management are separate protections.
